The studio was called "Eternal Serenity," a name that felt increasingly ironic as Jim, a man whose idea of stretching was reaching for the remote, sat in the back row. He had intended to join the "Gentle Morning Flow," but due to a misread schedule and a profound lack of spatial awareness, he had walked into the "Advanced Inversion & Breath Control" class.

The instructor, a woman named Seraphina who looked like she had been carved from marble and patience, began the session with a whisper. "Inhale the universe. Exhale your ego."

Jim inhaled. He also inhaled a significant amount of dust from the carpet. He sneezed. It was a small, polite sneeze, but in the silence of the room, it sounded like a gunshot.

Seraphina didn’t flinch. "Good. Now, let us move into the Pose of the Long Neck."

Jim looked around. Everyone else was standing on their hands or balancing on one toe. He looked at his own neck. It was average. Perhaps slightly thick from years of looking at spreadsheets. He decided to interpret "Long Neck" literally. He craned his head forward, stretching his neck muscles until he looked like a confused swan trying to escape a net.

"Excellent alignment, Jim," Seraphina said, gliding over. "Now, deepen the stretch. Let your body become fluid."

Jim tried to be fluid. He shifted his weight. The movement was subtle, but it was enough to dislodge the large, spicy burrito he had eaten for lunch in a desperate attempt to feel full despite his anxiety.

A sound emerged from Jim. It was not a grunt. It was not a sigh. It was a low, resonant *toot* that echoed off the bamboo walls. It lasted for three seconds. It had a distinct vibrato.

The class froze. Ten people were holding complex poses, their faces masks of concentration, now shattered by the sheer audacity of the noise.

Seraphina paused. She looked at Jim. Jim looked at Seraphina. Jim’s face was the color of a ripe tomato. He tried to cover it up by making a louder noise, so he let out a second, higher-pitched squeak.

"Ah," Seraphina said, her voice calm as a still pond. "The body speaks when the mind is too loud. This is the Pose of the Unfiltered
